name: Botox for underarm sweat

lead: Botox for underarm sweat gives months of dry underarms: no sweat marks on shirts and less moisture for odor to build on.

The toxin blocks release of acetylcholine from nerve endings, so the nerves stop telling sweat glands to produce sweat. Reference sources describe it as an approved option for severe underarm sweating that topical products have not controlled. The effect is reported to last about 3 to 9 months before repeat injections. Research has focused on axillary hyperhidrosis rather than odor.

paras: A clinician injects the armpit skin in a short office visit, often after topical antiperspirants have not been enough. Results last months and treatment is repeated as the effect wears off.

Injections can be painful, and ice is sometimes used for comfort. General botulinum toxin warnings include spread of effect to nearby muscles. The effect is temporary, so ongoing sessions mean ongoing cost.

angle.text: Clinic-delivered botulinum toxin injections switch off underarm sweat glands for months, giving dry shirts and less odor. It is studied for axillary hyperhidrosis, with limited research on odor specifically.

lead: Botulinum toxin injections for underarm sweat place a neurotoxin into the skin of the armpit to reduce excessive sweating (axillary hyperhidrosis). The looks payoff is dry underarms: no sweat rings or visible damp patches on shirts, less yellowing and staining of clothing, and more freedom to wear fitted or light-coloured clothes. The toxin blocks release of acetylcholine from nerve endings, the signal that tells sweat glands to produce sweat.[1][2]

The American Academy of Dermatology describes botulinum toxin as FDA approved for hyperhidrosis, with most patients noticing less sweating within 7 to 10 days and results for the underarms or hands lasting about 3 to 10 months.[3] Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article describes it as an option for severe underarm sweating that topical treatments have not controlled, and lists injection pain as a drawback.[2]

On T Nation, members mention it as the option that worked after other measures failed; one reports no sweat for two years and gives a rough annual cost, and another asks about reported lab-animal findings on toxin spread.[4][5][6] Published trial material in the record includes a small registered trial of botulinum toxin with suction-curettage.[7]
infobox: FDA approved for hyperhidrosis per AAD[3]

paras: Botulinum toxin type A cleaves proteins involved in nerve-ending signalling and so prevents acetylcholine release, producing temporary paralysis of muscle in its better-known cosmetic uses [1]. In hyperhidrosis the same blockade of nerve signals to sweat glands reduces sweat output [2].

Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article describes botulinum toxin as used for severe underarm sweating that topical treatments cannot manage, notes that the first non-muscular use of the toxin was reported in 1993, and lists pain at injection as a drawback [2].

The AAD lists pain, bruising, headache, muscle soreness or weakness at the injection site and mild itching as the most common side effects, and says studies show the treatment can be safe and effective. It advises stopping aspirin, certain anti-inflammatory drugs and vitamin E before treatment to lower bruising risk.[3]

Wikipedia's botulinum toxin article reports that in 2008 the FDA warned the toxin can spread from the injection site, especially in children with cerebral palsy, and that boxed warnings were announced in 2009. It also notes the FDA approved Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines in 2002.[1]

T Nation threads from 2008 to 2010 include a reply that Botox injections can stop underarm sweating, a member who says nothing worked until Botox and that the cost was about 500 dollars a year, and a thread titled 'Finally Got My Botox' where a reply explains that the thread concerns excessive underarm sweating specifically rather than sweating in general.[4][5][8] Another poster considering the injections cites lab-animal research that toxin can travel along neurons from the injection site and asks about it; those are the member's reading of studies, not clinical findings in people.[6]

A small registered trial (NCT01274611, 20 participants, started 2010) examined botulinum toxin together with suction-curettage for axillary hyperhidrosis [7]. Results are not summarised in the available record. Beyond this, the reviewed material does not include other trial data for this entry.

General reference sources list injection pain and the possibility of unintended spread of toxin effect to nearby muscles as recognised issues of botulinum toxin treatment [1][2]. Effects are temporary, so treatment is repeated.

lore.intro: Underarm Botox appears in T Nation threads on sweating and body odour, usually as a last-resort option after antiperspirants and clothing choices.[4][5][8]

claims.claim: Botox stops underarm sweating for long stretches.
The toxin can travel to the brain.

timeline.event: Richard Clark reports botulinum toxin for forehead wrinkles after a facelift complication.[1]
First non-muscular use of botulinum toxin reported, as described in reference summaries of hyperhidrosis treatment [2].
FDA approves Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines.[1]
Boxed warnings announced for botulinum toxin products after spread concerns.[1]
